problems.memo_sentence: The approach reduces the constrained portfolio problem to a second-order cone program (SOCP) and then applies a quantum short-step interior-point method (IPM) for SOCPs as the main algorithmic engine.
problems.source_evidence: Our algorithm for constrained portfolio optimization first reduces the problem to second order cone programs (SOCP)... We then use a recently developed quantum interior point method for SOCPs [20]... However, the running time of all these quantum algorithms depends on a number of problem specific parameters and they do not achieve a worst case speedup over classical algorithms.
problems.explanation: The memo presents the SOCP+quantum IPM route as the main engine without reflecting the paper's explicit caveat that the quantum speedup is not worst-case and depends on problem-specific parameters.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors emphasize that, unlike the unconstrained case, this general constrained problem lacks a closed-form solution and thus requires algorithmic treatment.
problems.source_evidence: For the case when there are no inequality constraints, the problem becomes a linear least-squares problem, for which there is a closed-form solution [27]. However, there is no closed form solution for the general constrained portfolio optimization problem.
problems.explanation: The memo omits the paper's explicit limitation that the closed-form solution exists only in the no-inequality-constraints case, which is the contrast the authors make.

problems.memo_sentence: The main theoretical result guarantees that the algorithm outputs a portfolio whose objective value is within εr of the optimum and that satisfies inequality constraints exactly and equality constraints to precision δ, with a running time given as T = Õ(√r log(n/ε) · n κ ζ / δ² log(κζ/δ)).
problems.source_evidence: Theorem 5.1... (ii) Te solution satisfies the inequality constraints x ≥0, the equality constraints are satisfied approximately to precision δ... (iii) Te running time for the algorithm is ... where κ = maxi ∈[T ] κi is the maximum condition number of the Newton matrix (6) over the T = O(√r log(n/ϵ)) iterations and ζ ≤ √n is a parameter that appears in the quantum linear system solver.
problems.explanation: The memo states the theorem but drops the dependence on the condition number being the maximum over iterations and the bound ζ ≤ √n, both of which are part of the same result and materially qualify the runtime claim.

problems.memo_sentence: The classical baseline is the short-step interior-point method for SOCPs, whose convergence to ε-duality gap is established with time complexity O(√r n^ω log(ν₀/ε)), often approximated as O(n^3.5 log(n/ε)) in practice, and whose cost is dominated by solving dense linear systems.
problems.source_evidence: Te time complexity for this algorithm is O(√rn^ω log(ν0/ϵ)) where ω < 2.37 is the exponent for matrix multiplication. In practice the running time for the constrained portfolio optimization problem is O(n3.5 log(ν0/ϵ)) as r = O(n) if positivity constraints are included and the algorithms for matrix inversion requires time O(n3) in practice.
problems.explanation: The memo collapses the classical complexity into a generic dense-linear-system story and omits the paper's specific condition that the O(n^3.5) estimate comes from r = O(n) when positivity constraints are included.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors stress that translating theoretical quantum speedups in mathematical finance into real-world use will require much more advanced hardware than currently available, highlighting a practical deployment limitation.
problems.source_evidence: Of course, translating these theoretical advantages of quantum algorithms into real world applications necesitates both much more advanced hardware, which may take some more years to come, but also a close collaboration between the communities of quantum algorithms and of mathematical Finance...
problems.explanation: The memo captures the hardware limitation, but not the paper's additional limitation that real-world deployment also requires close collaboration between quantum algorithms and mathematical finance communities.

problems.memo_sentence: The authors also prove that approximate Newton updates preserve strict feasibility and decrease the duality gap by a constant factor, and that infeasibility of the final iterate is bounded by the tomography precision; empirically, they observe that worst-case condition number growth is not attained, that tomography precision requirements scale roughly linearly with n, and that for most tested instances the quantum algorithm exhibits an almost O(n) speedup with an empirically fitted complexity exponent supporting this behaviour.
problems.source_evidence: Figure 5 shows how this quantity increases with the problem size n, after removing 1% of the biggest outliers. Again, by finding the least-squares fit of a power law through these points, one obtains a dependence of O(n2.387), with a 95% confidence bound of [2.184, 2.589]. Terefore, for most instances, we obtain an almost O(n)-speedup over the practical O(n3.5) complexity of the classical algorithm.
problems.explanation: The memo reports the near-linear speedup but omits the paper's explicit empirical caveat that the fitted average-case complexity is O(n^2.387), not O(n), and that this is after removing outliers.
